turns.doctor_question: Hello, and welcome. I'm Dr. [Name], a psychiatrist. What brings you in to see me today?
turns.patient_response:
Hi, Doctor. Um, well, I guess what brings me in is that I'm just losing hours of my day to rechecking things. I'm an engineer, so I'm used to being thorough, but... this is different. I keep checking and rechecking file dimensions, my revision notes, and even stuff at home, like my dressing supplies or the door locks. 

It's like I don't feel allowed to just move on to the next task. I have to go through the exact same checking routine enough times until... well, until the anxiety finally drops. It's just taking up way too much of my life right now, and I need to figure out how to stop.

symptom_reasoning.S066: The patient reports spending hours repeatedly performing checking routines on items like door locks, dressing supplies, and work files to alleviate anxiety before they feel able to move on.

turns.doctor_question: Before you feel the urge to check these things, do you notice specific thoughts or worries popping into your head that feel intrusive or unwanted — like thoughts that something bad might happen if you don't check? Or is it more of a general sense of unease that leads you to check?
turns.patient_response: It's definitely specific thoughts, not just a general unease. Um, for example, even after I know I’ve cleaned the wound area, or... or reviewed a CAD file at work, this thought just keeps cutting in. It's always this worry that I missed one tiny thing, and that it’s going to turn into a bad infection, or a design mistake that ends up actually hurting someone. And the frustrating part is that no matter how much logic I use, I just... I can’t seem to reason it away.

symptom_reasoning.S065: The patient explicitly confirms recurrent, intrusive, and unwanted thoughts of doubt and catastrophe (fearing an infection or hurting someone) that persist despite attempts to reason them away.

turns.doctor_question: When you feel that anxiety from the intrusive thought, does the checking actually help bring the anxiety down, or does the anxiety eventually go away on its own even without checking?
turns.patient_response:
Well, I'm not entirely sure if it would ever just go away on its own. I don't think I've ever really... just waited it out without checking. The anxiety gets so intense that I always end up giving in and doing the routine. 

When I do check, yeah, it definitely brings the anxiety down. It gives me this sense of relief, but it's only temporary before the whole thing starts over again. So I guess I don't really know what would happen if I just didn't do it.

symptom_reasoning.S066: The patient explicitly confirms performing repetitive checking routines to relieve intense anxiety, providing temporary relief before the cycle repeats.

turns.doctor_question: When you have these intrusive thoughts about missing something or causing harm, how much distress do they cause you just from having the thought itself — separate from the anxiety about what might actually happen if you don't check?
turns.patient_response: Um, well, like I mentioned a minute ago about the CAD files or the wound cleaning... the thought itself is really upsetting just because of how stubborn it is. It's incredibly frustrating. I know logically that I did the work right, but that worry just forces its way into my head anyway. The fact that I can't just reason it away or shut the thought off... that alone causes a lot of distress, even before I start panicking about the actual consequences of someone getting hurt. It just makes me feel like I can't trust my own brain.

symptom_reasoning.S065: The patient describes intrusive, unwanted thoughts forcing their way into their mind that cannot be reasoned away or shut off, causing significant distress.

turns.doctor_question: When you think about your day overall, would you say the checking rituals themselves are the main problem that bothers you and takes up your time, or is it more that these intrusive thoughts keep popping up and forcing you to check in order to manage them?
turns.patient_response:
I think it's really the checking rituals themselves that are the main problem. The thoughts are upsetting, sure, but what actually brings me in here is that I'm losing hours of my day to rechecking things. 

It's the dressing supplies, door locks, the file dimensions at work, my revision notes... I just get stuck. I don't feel like I'm allowed to move on to the next thing until I've gone through the exact same checking routine enough times. I have to keep doing it until that anxiety finally drops. So it's the time I lose to the actual checking that really bothers me the most.

symptom_reasoning.S066: The patient explicitly confirms spending hours each day performing repetitive checking routines (locks, supplies, work files) to relieve anxiety before they can move on.

turns.doctor_question: If you could somehow make the intrusive thoughts about missing something or causing harm just disappear completely — but still had to do the checking routines — would that be a major relief for you, or would you still feel just as stuck by having to do all the checking?

Um, I'm not really sure how to answer that. It's... it's kind of hard to picture. I mean, the thoughts are what trigger the checking for me in the first place. 

But if you're saying I still had to spend all those hours doing the actual routines anyway... I think I'd still feel pretty stuck. Because, like I said, it's the time I lose to checking the files and the locks that really messes up my day. So... yeah, I don't really know if it would be a major relief if I was still losing all that time. I guess I just haven't ever thought about it like that.
